name: Azure APIM secrets
tile_line: Stolen secrets stay valid after Microsoft's fix.
tldr: A flaw let attackers read secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic until Microsoft blocked it on 19 Nov 2026, and Norway's NSM ties it to attacks. On a Classic tier (not Consumption), rotate what APIM stored: the block doesn't cancel stolen keys.
summary: Microsoft says the flaw let an unauthorized party reach admin functions in Classic-tier instances; it found the flaw on 18 Nov 2026. Norway's NSM links it to attacks on Equinor and Skagerak Energi (Skagerak calls its case an attempt with no impact) and says it affects several sectors in Norway and beyond.

affected.label: You run an APIM Classic tier
affected.text: Microsoft says Classic tiers were affected and v2 tiers were not; Microsoft's docs list the Classic tiers as Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium, with Consumption separate. NSM says v2 and Consumption tier instances aren't vulnerable. Customers told The Register that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organisations exposed.

affected.label: Not locked down before 19 Nov
affected.text: Microsoft says exposure was tied to Classic instances that didn't follow its network security guidance or that stored secrets directly in APIM instead of referencing Azure Key Vault. A researcher's write-up says instances whose endpoints couldn't be reached from the internet (a private endpoint, or an internal virtual network with public access off) weren't exposed to this route; a firewall in front only helps if attackers couldn't reach APIM directly. NSM makes no such exception: it tells everyone with APIM to assume their secrets and named values are exposed, and Kristiansen notes Key Vault references don't protect a value from someone who can edit policies or use tracing.

do.label: Check your instance got the fix
do.text: NSM's check: open this address on your gateway, from a network that can reach it, and read `RuntimeVersion`. On 0.52.x you're patched if the last number is 31936 or higher, on 0.53.x if it's 31938 or higher. Other patterns (such as `0.53.4608.0`) are v2 or Consumption tier and not vulnerable. If yours is lower, NSM says to contact your provider directly. Microsoft says its own fix needed no customer action; it's unclear whether NSM's version thresholds and that fix are the same thing.

do.label: Rotate what APIM stored
do.text: Microsoft lists what may have been exposed: secrets in named values, client secrets for identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens for the direct management API. Its fix "does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed". NSM says to assume secrets and named values are out and rotate all tokens and secrets. Anders Kristiansen's write-up adds backend credentials, app registration secrets, the Key Vault secrets APIM references and the tenant access keys.

do.label: Check what sits behind APIM
do.text: A stolen credential may work directly against the service it protects, outside APIM. NSM says to map what information sits behind each instance; Microsoft says to look for suspicious activity in systems those credentials reach and to review your logs. An admin's Reddit post, cited by BleepingComputer, says attackers logged in to their Key Vaults with a valid administrator token; BleepingComputer hasn't verified it.

do.label: Turn off the old management API
do.text: Each instance has a direct management API at `https://<service-name>.management.azure-api.net`. Microsoft retired it on 15 March 2025 and says to disable it if it's on. In the portal that's Management API, Enable Management REST API: No. Two researchers' write-ups say it bypasses Entra ID and Azure role checks and its calls don't show in the Activity log; msandbu's write-up names it as the attack route and says it was still active even when set to No. The Reddit admin quoted by BleepingComputer says attackers used an authentication bypass in "a deprecated legacy API" (not verified). Microsoft hasn't confirmed how the attacker got in.

do.label: Microsoft hasn't published details
do.text: Microsoft's advisory (Azure Service Health, tracking ID MZK9-GH0) went to customers and isn't public; there's no CVE yet, and it isn't on CISA's list of exploited bugs. NSM says it's still unclear how widely the flaw was exploited. We'll check again by 1 Dec 2026.

versions_skip: Azure API Management is a hosted service that Microsoft fixed on its side on 19 Nov 2026; there's nothing for customers to install.
